data.label: Interaction Challenges in Human-Robot Space Exploration

publicationNotes.notes: A broad framing paper for why future exploration missions need effective human-robot teams. Useful for identifying interaction challenges and mission tasks where robots reduce workload, cost, fatigue, and risk.
publicationNotes.notesHtml:
A broad framing paper for why future exploration missions need effective human-robot teams.

  • Use as the map's entry point for space HRI challenges.
  • Connects workload, fatigue, autonomy, and sustainable exploration.
  • Good seed for literature questions about team effectiveness.
publicationNotes.citation: Fong, T. W., & Nourbakhsh, I. (2005). Interaction Challenges in Human-Robot Space Exploration. Interactions, 12(2), 42-45.
publicationNotes.abstract: This paper describes exploration tasks that could be performed by human-robot teams and identifies interaction challenges that must be addressed to make such teams effective.

data.label: Affordance-based task communication for astronaut-robot cooperation

publicationNotes.notes: Compares direct task communication with affordance-based indirect communication for astronaut-robot cooperation. Good anchor for interface design and workload reduction.
publicationNotes.notesHtml:
Compares direct task communication with affordance-based indirect communication for astronaut-robot cooperation.

  • Relevant to speech and gesture interfaces embedded in suits.
  • Shows how indirect task communication can reduce communication time and workload.
  • Useful for EVA and planetary surface operations.
publicationNotes.citation: Heikkila, S. S., Halme, A., & Schiele, A. (2012). Affordance-based indirect task communication for astronaut-robot cooperation. Journal of Field Robotics, 29(4), 576-600.
publicationNotes.abstract: The paper evaluates affordance-based communication methods for astronaut-robot cooperation in planetary exploration style work contexts.

data.label: Autonomy for Space Robots: Past, Present, and Future

publicationNotes.notes: Review of autonomy across space mission phases. Useful background for deciding what level of autonomy is plausible for crew-facing robotic systems.
publicationNotes.notesHtml:
Review of autonomy across space mission phases.

  • Good background node for autonomy capability and limits.
  • Helps separate robotic autonomy from human-robot teaming questions.
  • Useful for future-work ideas around delay-tolerant supervised autonomy.
publicationNotes.citation: Nesnas, I. A. D., Fesq, L. M., & Volpe, R. A. (2021). Autonomy for Space Robots: Past, Present, and Future. Current Robotics Reports, 2, 251-263.
publicationNotes.abstract: A review of space autonomy advances, current practice, and future needs for space exploration.

data.label: The Space Between Us: Bridging Human and Robotic Worlds

publicationNotes.notes: Recent scoping-review direction for HRI in outer space exploration. Useful for identifying themes and literature gaps.
publicationNotes.notesHtml:
Recent scoping-review direction for HRI in outer space exploration.

  • Good modern synthesis node.
  • Useful for turning a demo map into a PhD literature review plan.
publicationNotes.citation: Patel, D. D., & Geiskkovitch, D. Y. (2024). The Space Between Us: Bridging Human and Robotic Worlds in Space Exploration. Companion of the ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction, 833-836.
publicationNotes.abstract: A scoping-review oriented paper identifying interconnected themes in space human-robot interaction research.

data.label: Robot support as crew health and performance protection
data.documentHtml:
Frame HRI as a bioastronautics problem: robots are not only tools, they are countermeasures against crew overload, fatigue, time pressure, and operational risk.

  • Question: which robot behaviors measurably protect crew health and performance?
  • Useful outcomes: workload, stress, situation awareness, error risk, and crew time.

data.label: Robots as workload buffers during long-duration missions
data.documentHtml: Long-duration missions need robotic systems that absorb routine monitoring, logistics, documentation, and setup tasks so crew attention can stay on science, health, and off-nominal decisions.

data.label: Trust calibration matters more than raw autonomy
data.documentHtml: For mission use, the question is not simply whether a robot is autonomous. Crew must understand what the robot can do, when to supervise it, and when to take over.

data.label: Shared control must adapt to communication delay
data.documentHtml: Future Moon and Mars operations require interfaces that support local crew autonomy and delayed ground support. Shared control should shift based on latency, task risk, and crew workload.

data.label: IVA, EVA, and surface habitats need different HRI patterns
data.documentHtml: Intravehicular assistants, suited EVA assistants, and planetary surface robots impose different constraints on speech, gesture, mobility, proximity, and autonomy.

data.label: Function allocation is a human-system trade space
data.documentHtml: Robot roles should be assigned by modeling crew performance, workload, risk, and mission constraints, not by assuming that automation is always preferable.

data.label: Analog testing gap: lab HRI does not capture mission constraints
data.documentHtml: A PhD plan should identify what can be tested in lab studies, what needs analog missions, and what metrics transfer to real spaceflight operations.

data.notes: Fong and Nourbakhsh frame different exploration tasks where human-robot interaction patterns diverge.
Workload, fatigue, and risk connect space HRI directly to crew health and performance.
Affordance-based communication suggests how astronauts can issue task requests without exhaustive parameter entry.
Speech and gesture interaction requirements are especially relevant for suited field work.
Autonomy capability must be paired with supervision, transparency, and appropriate crew trust.
Deep-space autonomy becomes more important as communication delay increases.
NASA's HRS framing supports the idea that robots should help humans operate more effectively.
Astrobee is a concrete example of task offloading inside a spacecraft habitat.
IVA free-flying robots have different HRI constraints than EVA or surface systems.
The TechPort project is a direct anchor for modeling crew-robot function allocation.
Task allocation should be evaluated by its impact on crew workload and mission performance.
A scoping review helps expose what HRI findings still need mission-relevant validation.
Trust is one likely cross-cutting theme for future space HRI research.
Crew workload buffering is one measurable way to operationalize a bioastronautics HRI argument.
Function-allocation methods need validation settings that preserve mission constraints.
